text:
The Beatles stunned onlookers when they pitched up on the rooftop of 3 Savile Row in London in 1969 for their final public performance, but now Westminster city council is seeking to ban live music being played there ahead of plans to convert the site into a tourist attraction.
On Tuesday, councillors will vote on proposals to turn the Grade-II listed building in Mayfair into a seven-storey “cultural experience and exhibition” commemorating the history and legacy of the Fab Four.
Apple Corps, the intellectual property company established by the Beatles in 1968, re-acquired the building – which was the band’s headquarters between 1968 and 1972 – in May, announcing plans to open it to the public as a visitor attraction in 2027.
Westminster council set out a number of conditions for its approval as a visitor attraction, including terms ensuring any amplified audio would have to be controlled through noise limiters, and imposing a restriction on live music on the rooftop to avoid “unacceptable noise levels”. The installation of a 2-metre-high acoustic barrier has also been proposed.
But the plans have faced opposition from businesses on the street, renowned as the heart of British tailoring. The Savile Row Bespoke Association, an organisation representing the area’s tailors, said the street’s narrow pavements “would lead to dangerous congestion and have a significant negative impact on those who visit and work” there.
Planning officers said the proposed changes clashed with local land use policies, but that the building’s unique connection to the Beatles warranted an exception.
Apple Corps said the attraction, which would include a cafe-bar and an exhibition shop, could attract up to 900 visitors on weekdays and 1,140 visitors at weekends, but the Mayfair Neighbourhood Forum said the number of tourists would “need to be greatly reduced” and requested that the planned attraction be monitored for 12 months before an expansion.
The proposed attraction would feature a re-creation of the studio where the band recorded the album Let it Be, as well as giving fans access to the rooftop where the famous concert took place. Items from the Apple Corps archives would also be on show alongside temporary exhibitions.
Paul McCartney called the plans “terrific”.
“Tourists come to England and … go to Abbey Road, but they can’t go inside [the studios] – it snares up the traffic and the drivers get really annoyed,” he said.
Tom Greene, the chief executive of Apple Corps, said: “Every single day, fans are taking pictures of the outside of 3 Savile Row – but next year they can go in.
“Even the railings remain the same from that famous day in 1969.”
On 30 January 1969, the Beatles played their last public concert on 3 Savile Row’s rooftop to an audience on the street, before the Metropolitan police arrived and ordered them to reduce the volume.
Over a 42-minute set, the band played songs from the final album they recorded together, Let it Be, including Get Back, Don’t Let Me Down, I’ve Got a Feeling and Dig a Pony, as well as an impromptu jam of the national anthem.
The performance was documented in The Beatles: Get Back (2021), an eight-hour documentary series released by Disney which reworked footage from Michael Lindsay-Hogg’s 1970 film, Let it Be.

מועצת העיר וסטמינסטר בלונדון צפויה להצביע על שורה של הגבלות ותנאים לקראת הפיכת הבניין ההיסטורי ברחוב סביל רואו לאתר תיירות ומרכז תרבות לזכר להקת הביטלס. האתר, הידוע כמקום שבו קיימה הלהקה את הופעתה הפומבית האחרונה על הגג בשנת 1969, נרכש מחדש על ידי חברת אפל קורפ במטרה לפתוח אותו למבקרים בשנת 2027 עם שחזור של אולפני ההקלטות ותצוגות ארכיון.

במסגרת אישור הפרויקט, הרשויות דורשות להטיל איסור מוחלט על השמעת מוזיקה חיה על גג הבניין במטרה למנוע מפגעי רעש לסביבה, לצד הגבלות על עוצמת הקול והתקנת מחסומים אקוסטיים. התוכנית מעוררת התנגדות מצד עסקים מקומיים ואיגודי חייטים באזור החוששים מעומסי תנועה ומצפיפות ברחובות הצרים, אך חברת אפל קורפ ומעריצים רבים רואים במיזם הזדמנות מבורכת שתוסדר בפיקוח הדוק.
